analysis.one_liner: Rewrites and renews the Clean Water Act, with more sewage-treatment funding, toxic pollution controls, and beach monitoring.
analysis.headline: The Senate Environment Committee reported this clean water overhaul in May 1994 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but the bill never came up for a vote before the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This was a comprehensive renewal of the Clean Water Act. It would have sent billions more in federal loans to towns to fix sewage systems, given small and low-income communities easier terms, required big industrial polluters to prevent toxic waste at the source, cleaned up runoff from farms and streets, and required states to monitor bacteria at beaches and warn swimmers. It also eased some wetlands permitting rules for landowners and developers. It was reported out of committee but never got a Senate vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who swim in or eat fish from polluted waters, towns that need to fix aging sewers (the bill cites an estimated $130 billion need [S3]), small and low-income communities that would get technical help and possible loan forgiveness [S2][S3], tribes [S2], and Great Lakes, Gulf, and Chesapeake communities whose regional programs would be reauthorized [S2]. Recreational and subsistence fishers would get federal guidance on contaminants in fish and shellfish so states can issue consumption advisories [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes $2.5 billion per year through 2000 for state revolving loan funds that finance sewage treatment construction, with more if deficit targets are met [S3].
Lets states forgive loan principal for disadvantaged communities and gives small treatment systems (serving 10,000 or fewer people) technical assistance that can offset state matching costs [S2][S3].
Requires EPA to publish guidance on contaminants in fish and shellfish so states can warn recreational and subsistence fishers [S2].
Requires states to monitor pathogens at coastal beaches during use, notify the public of violations, and adopt standards for marine recreational waters [S2].

Prioritizes source reduction in industrial effluent limits and pretreatment standards, and requires pollution prevention plans for facilities releasing over 200,000 pounds of toxic chemicals annually [S2].
Strengthens control of farm and street runoff through watershed plans and lets EPA withhold up to half of program funds from states that fail to act [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Industrial dischargers that would face stronger pretreatment standards, source-reduction requirements, and pollution prevention planning; taxpayers who would fund the new authorizations; and states, which would have to shoulder a rising share of matching costs (up to 50 percent) for program grants [S3]. Landowners and developers would face wetlands permitting, though the bill eases several of those rules [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes billions in new federal spending (up to $5 billion a year in later years if deficit conditions are met), a real cost in a deficit-focused era [S3].
Its wetlands title eases regulation: general nationwide permits, an exemption for prior converted croplands, permit decision deadlines, and appeal rights for landowners [S2].

It authorizes temporary waivers of permit limits and pretreatment standards (up to 90 days, with extensions) to test innovative technologies, which environmental groups would view as risky openings [S2].
State matching shares for program grants rise from 30 percent to 50 percent, shifting costs onto state budgets [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health and environmental gains — cleaner beaches, fish advisories, toxic source reduction, and money for sewage systems towns cannot afford — outweigh the fiscal cost, and the bill tied added spending to deficit conditions. The main honest criticism is that the wetlands provisions trade away some protection for permitting speed, and the technology waivers add enforcement uncertainty.

outcome.mechanism: The committee reported the bill and it sat on the Senate calendar, but the Senate never voted on it before the 103rd Congress ended.

narrative.text: The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee ordered an original bill reported on February 25, 1994, in lieu of S. 1114 [S5].
Chairman Max Baucus reported the measure on May 10, 1994, with written report 103-257; additional and minority views were filed [S5].
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 424 on May 10, 1994 [S5].
The only later entries are sponsor introductory remarks in May and June 1994; no floor action was ever taken before the 103rd Congress ended January 3, 1995 [S5].
Republicans won majorities in both chambers in the November 1994 elections, and the incoming 104th Congress took no up the bill; no comprehensive Clean Water Act reauthorization became law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industrial dischargers and large landowners facing the bill's new pollution-prevention and runoff requirements, and municipal polluters, all kept the status quo. Towns awaiting sewer money and swimmers and fishers awaiting better warnings gained nothing, since the funding and monitoring never happened.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a Democratic chairman's committee product filed with minority views, drew zero cosponsors [S4], and died with a Senate controlled by Democrats until the Republicans won the 1994 elections; no vote ever split the chambers by party.

industries.industry: Industrial polluters (chemical, pulp and paper, food processing and other dischargers)
industries.note: The bill requires pretreatment standards for pollutants sent to public treatment works, prioritizes source reduction in effluent limits, bans hazardous waste dumping into treatment works without conditions, and requires pollution prevention plans for facilities releasing over 200,000 pounds of toxics a year [S2]. Compliance would cost these firms money; the bill died so the requirements never took effect.

industries.industry: Real estate developers and large landowners
industries.note: Wetlands permitting would be streamlined with general permits, deadlines, appeal rights, and exemptions for prior converted croplands [S2], but delineation and permitting rules would still apply. Their interest ran toward weaker regulation, and the bill's wetlands title delivered part of that while its fate left everything unchanged.

Towns would get larger revolving loan funds, combined sewer overflow funding, loan forgiveness for disadvantaged communities, and technical help for small systems [S2][S3]. Cheaper sewage upgrades mean lower user fees for residents.

Farm runoff would face watershed-based control measures, and EPA must approve animal waste facility designs [S2]; in exchange, conservation compliance plans could substitute for new site-specific plans and USDA would delineate wetlands on agricultural land under a looser approach [S2].

Multi-year authorizations of $2.5 billion a year for loan funds [S3] and combined sewer overflow construction aid [S2] would fund construction work, with prevailing-wage standards extended to contract employees on funded projects [S2].

The bill formally establishes mitigation banks — restoration projects that sell credits to offset permitted wetlands losses [S2] — creating a market that helps permitting go faster but can shift wetlands losses to other locations.
